lessons.title: Why every organization needs an AI policy
lessons.subtitle: Shadow AI, Article 4, one document

sections.title: The shadow AI problem
sections.content:
> **At work:** This block is for people who implement or govern AI use in an organization. The template is a starting point. Jurisdiction, sector, worker representation, contracts and existing security rules you add yourself.

The sales lead runs a meeting bot. The working student has a browser extension, the assistant the new writing feature. Nobody asked. That is shadow AI: services or functions outside the approved inventory and the intended controls. Browser extensions, embedded writing features, meeting bots and local models create the same unknown data flows.

A policy turns that into a reviewable frame. Which purposes are allowed, which systems and features approved? Which data, recipients and decisions are involved, and who reviews new cases and handles incidents?

The document alone prevents nothing. It works once it is tied to inventory, technical controls, training, procurement, data protection, information security and an approval process people can reach.
sections.keyTakeaway: Shadow AI grows outside the approved inventory and the intended controls. A policy works only with named owners, technical controls and a usable approval process.

sections.title: The obligation: Article 4 since February 2025
sections.content:
Article 4 of the EU AI Act has applied since 2 February 2025. Not an outlook, but law in force. Since the amendment by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, providers and deployers must take measures supporting the development of AI literacy in their staff and other people dealing with the operation and use of AI systems on their behalf. Technical knowledge, experience, education and training, use context and the people or groups affected must be taken into account. What the Article does not require: a guaranteed level of competence for every individual, a standard attestation, a fixed training format.

What does that mean concretely? Providers and deployers need building blocks that can be traced. Roles, permitted tools, data rules, review routines, escalation, documented training. The AI policy is an important part of that.

Complete evidence under Article 4 the policy is not. It records which tools are approved, which data may go where, how outputs are checked and what happens after an incident. Depending on the use case, training, inventory, risk classification, data protection review and further internal processes come on top.
sections.keyTakeaway: Article 4 has applied since 2 February 2025. The AI policy is one documented building block of AI literacy measures, not complete evidence under Article 4.

quiz.questionText: Since when has Article 4 of the EU AI Act applied?

answerOptions.text: Since 1 January 2024
Since 2 February 2025
From August 2026
It is not in force yet

quiz.explanation: Since 2 February 2025. In its current form, providers and deployers must take measures supporting the development of AI literacy in people acting on their behalf. Not an announcement. It applies.

quiz.questionText: Which description of shadow AI is most accurate?

answerOptions.text: Only AI systems that run at night
Every local AI installation, approved ones included
AI services or functions used outside the approved inventory and intended controls
Only free chat services without user accounts

quiz.explanation: Price, provider, hosting location. None of it matters. Shadow AI sits outside the approved controls in use, purpose, data flow or accountability. An approved local installation is not shadow AI.

lessons.title: The six parts of your AI policy
lessons.subtitle: Six sections, one frame

sections.title: Parts 1 to 3: scope, tools and data
sections.content:
Six sections. The template claims no more. No compliance scheme complete everywhere. Depending on the use, procurement, copyright, product safety, high-risk duties, transparency, worker representation or export control come on top.

**1. Scope and definitions:** Which people, entities, systems, functions, and use types does the document cover?

**2. Inventory and approvals:** Which exact product version, feature, configuration, and integration is approved for which purpose? Who owns the decision?

**3. Data and decision rules:** Which data classes, rights, recipients, and impacts are permitted? Which uses are prohibited or require case-specific review?
sections.keyTakeaway: Scope, system approvals, data and decision rules. The first three sections. A product name fills none.

sections.title: Parts 4 to 6: review, escalation and maintenance
sections.content:
**4. Review and human responsibility:** Which controls apply at each impact level? Who may approve the result, and when is dual control or specialist legal, security, or domain review required?

**5. Incidents and escalation:** Which internal reporting channel applies? Which information and evidence must be preserved? Who assesses a data breach, security incident, faulty decision, or provider event?

**6. Ownership, changes, and review:** Who maintains the policy and inventory? Which events trigger immediate review? How are versions, approvals, and communication documented?

Length follows organization and risk. A short policy can be enough when inventory, approval matrix and operating procedures are maintained separately and linked without ambiguity.
sections.keyTakeaway: Parts 4 to 6 govern review, incidents and updating. All six build on the earlier blocks.

quiz.questionText: How many baseline sections does this course template use?

answerOptions.text: 3 parts
4 parts
6 parts
10 parts

quiz.explanation: Six. A scaffold to adapt, not a guarantee of legal or organizational completeness.

quiz.questionText: Which part of the AI policy rests directly on the three-step review from block 4?

answerOptions.text: Part 2: Approved tools
Part 3: Data rules
Part 4: Review requirement
Part 6: Review cycle

quiz.explanation: Part 4 carries the three baseline questions from block 4: factually correct, complete, appropriate. The policy then sets, by purpose and impact, review depth, approvers and additional controls.

sections.title: The template: scope, tools and data
sections.content:
Fill the template in with the responsible functions. Every bracketed placeholder is an open point.

**1. Scope:** [Organization] specifies which workers, contractors, sites, systems, functions, and work devices the policy covers. Link the definitions to the current AI inventory.

**2. Approval matrix:** For each entry, record the product, version or tier, feature, integration, purpose, data classes, responsible person, contract, region, retention, permissions, and approval date. Combinations of purpose, feature, and data class that are not listed stay blocked until they are reviewed. Price and brand are not control criteria.

**3. Data and decision rules:** Refer to the organization's classification policy. Add data minimization, rights in content, permitted recipients, prohibited secrets and credentials, and rules for decisions affecting people. And a route out of uncertainty people can reach.
sections.keyTakeaway: The approval matrix links purpose, feature, data class, contract, configuration and accountability. Free is not a security category. Neither is enterprise.

sections.title: Review requirement, escalation and signatures
sections.content:
**4. Review and approval:** Controls by impact: source checks, calculation verification, specialist approval, dual control, or a prohibition on automated decisions. And a name. The person who answers for the final result.

**5. Incident reporting:** Workers report suspected misuse without delay through [reporting channel] and preserve the time, system, account, input data, output, and actions already taken. Nobody deletes or alters evidence on their own. [Incident Response], information security, data protection, and other responsible functions assess the case under the existing procedure.

Where a personal data breach has occurred, the controller decides on the risk whether GDPR Article 33 requires notification to the supervisory authority. If so, without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours after becoming aware. Internal deadlines belong in the incident-response plan. This template invents no four- or 24-hour stages.

**6. Ownership and review:** Name [Policy Owner], the regular review date, and the events that trigger immediate review: new features, changed contracts, incidents, legal changes. Record the version, approvers, effective date, and communication. Who has to approve follows the organization's governance. Fixed signature roles do not exist.
sections.keyTakeaway: The policy names risk-based controls, a usable reporting channel, responsible decision-makers and documented review triggers.

quiz.questionText: Why does the policy prohibit free AI tools such as ChatGPT Free?

answerOptions.text: Because they deliver worse results than paid versions
Because unapproved consumer offers usually provide no DPA reviewed by the organization and no binding configuration for data use
Because they are available in English only
Because they need an internet connection

quiz.explanation: Not quality, not language, not the internet connection. Unapproved consumer offers usually leave the organization without a reviewed DPA, binding data controls and an agreed data region. Whether inputs flow into training depends on the product and its settings.

quiz.questionText: Which statement describes GDPR Article 33 correctly?

answerOptions.text: Every processing error must be reported externally within 24 hours
Only the employee involved decides whether notification is required
The controller assesses the risk; if notification is required, it is made without undue delay and where feasible within 72 hours after awareness
Notification is allowed only once the technical investigation is complete

quiz.explanation: Article 33 ties the duty to a personal data breach and the controller's risk assessment. The 72 hours run from awareness. No 24-hour duty exists for every processing error.

sections.title: Five documents, one system
sections.content:
Five documents, in your hands:

1. **AI inventory** with concrete functions, purposes, data, and owners.
2. **Example data classification** your organization still has to adapt.
3. **Four task patterns** for email, meetings, data analysis, and reports.
4. **Output review** as a starting point for risk-based controls.
5. **AI usage policy** linking everything else.

None of them is finished. A document is finished when the placeholders are replaced, the assumptions checked, the owners named and the approvals documented.
sections.keyTakeaway: Five working foundations, not finished documents. Review, named owners and documented approval make them usable.

sections.title: Next steps
sections.content:
The policy can be one documented building block of AI literacy measures under Article 4. Four steps first:

1. **Review and approve:** Bring in governance, data protection, information security, procurement and worker representation.
2. **Connect operations:** Link the inventory, approval matrix, technical controls, procurement, and incident response with unambiguous references.
3. **Teach by role:** The case worker, the team lead, the working student. Each applies permitted purposes, boundaries, review duties and the reporting channel.
4. **Control review:** Document a risk-based regular date and immediate review triggers.

Whether it works is not read off the signature. It shows when people find the right approval, when systems are bounded, and when incidents get reported. Actually reported, not merely reportable.
sections.keyTakeaway: Effectiveness comes from approved ownership, technical implementation, role-based application and documented reviews.

quiz.questionText: How many documents come out of the whole course?

answerOptions.text: 2 documents
3 documents
5 documents
8 documents

quiz.explanation: Five, one per block: AI inventory, data-classification card, prompt templates, three-step review and the AI usage policy.

quiz.questionText: What is the most important next step once the AI policy exists?

answerOptions.text: File the policy and dig it out when needed
Have the responsible functions review it, connect it to operations, teach it by role, and define review triggers
Wait until the EU issues further requirements
Hire an external consultant to implement it

quiz.explanation: In a folder it does nothing. A policy works when responsible functions approve it, controls implement it, people can apply it, and defined events trigger a review.
